newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal government squeaks past no-confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Nepal government squeaks past no-confidence vote.

text.p: Nepali Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's centre-right coalition narrowly survived a parliamentary no-confidence vote on Tuesday, officials said.
The communist opposition in the Himalayan kingdom came within two votes of obtaining the necessary majority in Nepal's lower house.
The Unified Marxist Leninist (UML) party garnered enough support from other parties to secure 101 votes compared to the 15-month-old government's 84.
But under Nepal's constitution the opposition needed to score 103 of the total 205 members of the lower house to carry a no-confidence motion against the government.

"Since the vote in favour of the motion is not a majority of the total number of members of the House of Representatives, I declare that the motion has been rejected in accordance with the constitution of 1990," Ram Chandra Poudel, speaker of the lower house, said.
The opposition alleged that the government had forcibly kept away deputies, including some of its own ministers, who were likely to vote against Deuba.
The prime minister on Monday denied any wrongdoing and said the ministers had gone to Bangkok for medical treatment.
The vote only went ahead after the government agreed that an all-party committee would probe into why a number of deputies were absent from the house for the vote.
The vote was the climax of a heated two-day debate which at times descended into chaos.

The communists and their allies at one stage held a sit-in in the central aisle of the house and snatched away the speaker's microphone, trying to halt efforts to push through the vote while some deputies were missing.
The no-confidence vote was precipitated by a split among junior partners in Deuba's three-party coalition.

Earlier this month 10 of 19 deputies of the Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), considered pro-monarchist, decided they could no longer support the coalition led by Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress, and allied themselves with the communists.
Deuba also lost the support of two members of the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP).
It is the second time in less than a year that Deuba has survived a no-confidence motion.
"I am very happy," a relieved Deuba told Reuters after the vote. He said he hoped to sort out differences within the coalition and that the split would be resolved.
He also said he planned to work more closely with the opposition to obtain good working relations.
But Devi Prasad Ojha, the UML chief whip, said Deuba should resign after Tuesday's numerical defeat.
"Since the government lost the majority it should step down," he said.
Before the split in the coalition ranks the governmenet controlled 108 of the 205 seats in the house and five seats were vacant.
